newsitem.title: THAILAND: FOCUS-Weak Thai finance results set gloomy scene.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Weak Thai finance results set gloomy scene.

text.p: Further poor Thai finance sector earnings released on Wednesday painted a gloomy picture of an industry wracked by liquidity problems and which could be on the verge of a solvency crisis, analysts said.
A second consecutive day of disappointing results saw the large but ailing General Finance and Securities Plc record a 1.8 billion ($57 million) baht loss in the first half.
Of the 18 finance and securities firms reporting half-year figures, only seven made a profit totalling 830 million baht.
That was easily dwarfed by the sector's losers who recorded cumulative losses of around 3.5 billion baht.
The losses reflected a continuing deterioration in asset quality as Thailand experiences its most severe economic crisis in more than a decade, analysts said.

Higher funding costs brought on by a liquidity squeeze, and losses on securities trading portfolios on the local stock market which hit 8-1/2 year lows in the second quarter, also squeezed bottom lines, they added.

"Generally the second quarter results were very poor... In my opinion the liquidity problems should continue during the second half of this year," said Suraphol Thipvilai, finance and securities sector analyst at Vickers Ballas.

As investor confidence has waned, many weaker firms have seen depositors withdraw promissory notes held at finance firms during the first half of the year and moved them either to the sector's strongest firms or into commercial banks.
The poor results helped dent the stock market index which fell 4.89 percent to 631.28 after grimly holding onto recent gains earlier on Wednesday.
They also helped batter the recently floated baht which sank to a record low of around 32.60 per dollar in the mid-afternoon before the central bank intervened.
A Bank of Thailand official said the pressure on the baht was partly due to the weak finance sector results.
"The concerns are now not so much liquidity as solvency. It's not a liquidity crisis any more it's a solvency crisis," said a senior foreign analyst at a local broker.
"Technically you can keep posting losses for years and years without a problem, but if you can't meet liabilities that is when firms become insolvent," he said.
Suspicions some firms have been accounting securities trading losses through balance sheets but not through profit and loss accounts was adding to such concerns, analysts said.
Of greatest concern is that the key banking sector appears to be showing the strain. The country's second largest commercial lender Krung Thai Bank Plc saw its half year profits tumble 37 percent.
Thai Military Bank Plc profits dipped 20 percent in the first six months to 1.832 billion baht against 2.3 billion in the corresponding period last year.
The possibility of further exposure of the banking sector to the kind of problems already facing many finance firms has made many investors nervous, analysts said.
The International Monetary Fund (IMF) on Monday called for strong medicine to tackle Thai problems before they worsened further.
Finance Minister Thanong Bidaya earlier on Wednesday promised a new set of measures was on its way on July 28 to bail out the troubled finance sector, but provided no details. ($1 = 31 baht)
